We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.
bullets: Mamba-2 state energy is nearly rank-one, but the useful output-read content lies in a different low-dimensional, non-coordinate-aligned subspace.
The proposed post-training method applies balanced truncation using full controllability and observability Gramians, with an exact rotation enabled by Mamba-2’s scalar-identity transition.
HARP allocates layer-specific ranks from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers instead of using uniform budgets.
Using one-pass calibration, the method halves state dimension with a 0.3-point average WikiText-2 perplexity increase across 130M–2.7B models, compared with 1.6 points for GHOST.
The approach is evaluated for perplexity and retrieval; performance degradation increases at 25% retention.
papers.selection_reason: Mamba-2 state compression reduces memory; fits memory efficiency.
papers.title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression
papers.tldr: Balanced state-subspace compression preserves Mamba-2’s input–output behavior better than coordinate-wise compression by targeting controllable and observable directions.

papers.abstract: Enabling a humanoid to interact naturally with human partners requires preserving not only individual motions but also the spatial, semantic, and contact relationships underlying the interaction (i.e., hugging, dancing, hand-shaking, etc.). Furthermore, a practical solution should generalize across various humanoid embodiments with distinct morphologies and kinematic constraints. To tackle this challenge, we propose HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that converts in-the-wild human-human interaction videos into physically plausible human-humanoid interactions. HumiTransfer first reconstructs 3D human motion with consistent foot-ground contact, then transfers one participant to a target humanoid embodiment via interaction modeling, using weighted joint-relative directions and anatomical offsets to prioritize interaction-critical inter-body relationships, while post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance. Subsequently, we apply HumiTransfer to 1,200 in-the-wild videos, producing approximately 500,000 frames of diverse interactions for the 26-DoF Unitree R1 Edu and the 23-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi humanoid robot, resulting in our HumiMimic dataset. Across both robots, HumiTransfer achieves superior motion fidelity, preserves inter-body relationships, and maintains contact accuracy compared with existing baselines. Moreover, we demonstrate that HumiMimic supports motion generation methods for synthesizing interactive humanoid motions following a human partner. Finally, our real robot deployments confirm the physical executability of the transferred motions in real-world settings.
authors: Nghia Le (Hann), Khang Nguyen (Hann), Ba Long Tran (Hann), Thi Quynh Nhu Pham (Hann), Binh Nguyen (Hann), Tuong Do (Hann), Erman Tjiputra (Hann), Hoan Nguyen (Hann), Tung D. Ta (Hann), Baoru Huang (Hann), Hai-Nguyen (Hann), Nguyen (Hann), Anh Nguyen
bullets: Addresses natural human-humanoid interaction across robots with different morphologies and kinematic constraints.
Reconstructs 3D human motion with foot-ground contact, then retargets one participant using interaction-aware joint directions and anatomical offsets.
Post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance.
Generates the HumiMimic dataset from 1,200 videos, covering about 500,000 frames for two humanoid platforms.
Experiments and real-robot deployments show improved motion fidelity, inter-body relationship preservation, contact accuracy, and physical executability over baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Transfers human-human interaction from in-the-wild videos to humanoid embodiments, directly relevant to learning from human video and robot learning.
papers.title: Mimetic Embodiment Transfer of Human-Humanoid Interaction from In-the-Wild Videos
papers.tldr: HumiTransfer converts in-the-wild human-human interaction videos into physically executable interactions for humanoid robots while preserving key spatial and contact relationships.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes over time (4D reconstruction) from a single moving camera is central to robotics and AR/VR applications, yet state-of the-art feed-forward methods rely solely on RGB frames and therefore inherit the failure modes of conventional cameras, including motion blur and temporal aliasing under fast or non-uniform camera and object motion. Event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously at microsecond resolution, offering a complementary signal that is largely immune to these artifacts, but whether this modality can be incorporated into existing RGB based 4D reconstruction pipelines without a full architectural redesign remains an open question. In this preliminary study, we investigate a minimal extension: we augment Monst3R, an existing RGB-only 4D reconstruction model, with an additional event-camera input branch, leaving the rest of the architecture unchanged. Across 3 benchmark datasets, this simple RGB-event fusion reduces Abs Rel by 3.4% on average relative to the RGB-only Monst3R baseline, and a sensitivity analysis shows that the improvement grows with the magnitude of camera and object motion, with the largest gains observed under high object motion conditions where RGB-only reconstruction degrades most. These early results suggest that even a lightweight, non-invasive fusion of event data can meaningfully improve 4D reconstruction robustness, motivating a more thorough architectural investigation in future work.
authors: Dulanga Weerakoon, Darshana Rathnayake, Van Minh Do, Hemanth Sabbella, Kaichen Zhou, Fangneng Zhan, Alok Prakash, Sanjay E. Sarma, Archan Misra, Paul Pu Liang
bullets: RGB-only 4D reconstruction can fail under motion blur and temporal aliasing.
The study augments Monst3R with an event-input branch while keeping its original architecture unchanged.
Across three benchmark datasets, RGB-event fusion reduces Abs Rel by 3.4% on average versus RGB-only Monst3R.
Improvements increase with motion magnitude and are largest under high object motion.
The preliminary results motivate deeper investigation of event-RGB fusion architectures.
papers.selection_reason: Fuses event cameras with RGB for dynamic 3D/4D reconstruction, directly relevant to 3D vision and robustness of scene reconstruction.
papers.title: 4D Reconstruction with Events & RGB
papers.tldr: Adding an event-camera branch to an RGB-only 4D reconstruction model improves robustness, especially during fast camera or object motion.

papers.abstract: Handheld data-collection interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) allow manipulation demonstrations to be gathered in the wild without a robot in the loop, but the quality of the resulting action labels is bounded by the accuracy of vision-based localization. Existing systems recover end-effector pose from monocular visual-inertial odometry, which is subject to scale ambiguity and drift, or delegate tracking to closed-source modules and external infrastructure that reintroduce cost and setup burden. We present OpenJaws, a fully open hardware and software framework for sensorized UMI that improves localization and simplifies deployment across robot platforms. OpenJaws pairs a modular, 3D-printed gripper exposing a standardized ISO adapter with a low-cost stereo camera to recover metric camera trajectories. We further introduce UMI-Loc-Bench-v1, a benchmark quantifying real-world localization accuracy for handheld data-collection devices, and show that stereo localization substantially outperforms monocular alternatives. Finally, we demonstrate that policies trained on data collected with OpenJaws can be deployed on a real robot across multiple tasks. Hardware, software, and data are released under a commercially permissive license. Code, data, and videos are available at https://open-jaws.github.io/
authors: Adithyavairavan Murali, Yash Oza, Karanbir Chahal, Neel Jawale, Silas De Vries, Hesam Rabeti, Erwin Coumans, Balakumar Sundaralingam, Stan Birchfield
bullets: Addresses scale ambiguity and drift in monocular UMI localization, while avoiding closed-source tracking systems and external infrastructure.
Combines a modular 3D-printed gripper with a standardized ISO adapter and a low-cost stereo camera.
Introduces UMI-Loc-Bench-v1 for evaluating real-world localization accuracy of handheld data-collection devices.
Reports that stereo localization substantially outperforms monocular alternatives.
Demonstrates robot policies trained with OpenJaws-collected data across multiple real-world tasks; hardware, software, and data are openly released.
papers.selection_reason: Open hardware UMI framework with stereo localization for collecting manipulation demonstrations; supports imitation learning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: OpenJaws: An Open Hardware UMI Framework with Stereo Localization for Generalist Manipulation
papers.tldr: OpenJaws is an open, low-cost stereo-tracked UMI framework that improves metric localization for collecting robot manipulation demonstrations and supports deployment across multiple tasks.

papers.abstract: Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.
authors: Chengxuan Pei, Ziyao Wang, Teng Mei, Zhe Li
bullets: Addresses the interface gap between generative language models and decision models that require explicit candidate lists.
Trains a formalizer on offline teacher-generated lists to construct validated alternatives from task context, while keeping the decision model frozen.
In CALVIN-D evaluations, formalization improved reported task success from 11.8% to 52.6% in a privileged-state setting.
A motivating comparison reported 46.5% success with pose candidates versus 11% with generic motions.
End-to-end latency was 2.09 s, compared with 3.67 s for Qwen3.5-27B under the stated experimental setting.
papers.selection_reason: Formalizer plus frozen decision model selects pose candidates for embodied tasks, evaluated on CALVIN-D task success.
papers.title: Learning to Formalize: Bridging Open-Ended Workloads and Fast Decision Models
papers.tldr: A small candidate-formalization model converts open-ended tasks into validated alternatives that a fast decision model can select, substantially improving success while maintaining low latency.

papers.abstract: Autonomous scientific agents must not only reason about experiments but also interact with the physical environments in which they are executed. Existing laboratory simulators typically rely on manually constructed assets and predefined procedures, while laboratory videos capture real equipment, layouts, and interactions but leave this information implicit in pixels. We introduce LabWorld, an agent-driven Real2Sim framework for reconstructing interactive 4D laboratory worlds from monocular RGB video. LabWorld recovers reusable 3D assets, a metric scene, time-varying object states, and procedure events. Multi-frame observations provide complementary evidence for asset and scene reconstruction, while motion reconstruction combines visual and geometric observations with event constraints encoding the spatial and temporal requirements of laboratory interactions. We evaluate LabWorld on real pipetting and vortexing videos collected in our laboratory against general-purpose agentic and dedicated reconstruction baselines. For pipetting, LabWorld achieves a mean Mask IoU of 0.501, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.033. For vortexing, it achieves a mean Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.035. On five pipetting videos, event-conditioned reconstruction increases the fraction of modeled physical constraints satisfied from 14.3% (5/35) to 100% (35/35). The resulting worlds expose geometry, motion, articulation, and events as explicit, editable state for replay, inspection, and future embodied scientific systems.
authors: Suozhi Huang, Kelsey Fu, Binxu Li, Luna Lyu, Kaize Wu, Wenbo Lu, David Smerkous, Jiahan Li, Siqi Zhu, Zhizhou Sha, Jiacheng Guo, Zhixuan Liang, Shilong Liu, Le Cong, Mengdi Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap between pixel-based laboratory videos and simulators with explicit, reusable equipment, scenes, object states, and procedure events.
Uses a Real2Sim pipeline that combines multi-frame visual evidence, geometric observations, and spatial-temporal event constraints.
Evaluated on real pipetting and vortexing videos, achieving Mask IoU of 0.501 and Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638.
Event-conditioned reconstruction increased satisfied modeled physical constraints from 14.3% to 100% across five pipetting videos.
Produces editable world states for replay, inspection, and future scientific agents; evaluation is scoped to pipetting and vortexing activities.
papers.selection_reason: Reconstructs interactive 4D laboratory worlds from monocular video, directly fitting 3D/4D scene and geometry reconstruction interests.
papers.title: LabWorld: Learning Interactive 4D Worlds for Scientific Experimentation
papers.tldr: LabWorld reconstructs editable, interactive 4D laboratory worlds from monocular videos to support embodied scientific experimentation.

papers.abstract: Low-precision training often relies on stochastic rounding (SR) to keep quantized gradients unbiased and prevent small updates from rounding to zero. Standard SR draws an independent random threshold for every gradient element. However, accelerators generate random numbers on vector units whose throughput lags far behind their matrix units. Drawing one threshold per element saturates the vector unit and can make INT8 training with SR slower than BF16 training. Sharing random thresholds across tensor elements removes this cost but forces those elements to round in the same direction and shifts their rounding errors by a common offset. We find that this offset degrades training primarily through the activation gradient, which propagates the error backward into earlier layers. Because earlier layers cannot cancel an incoming offset using their own local rounding errors, the offset must be removed at the layer where it originates. We propose Structured Subspace Stochastic Rounding (S3R), which quantizes each upstream gradient once for both the activation and weight gradient matrix multiplications and shares a single threshold per token across the hidden dimension. Its error correction, S3R-EC, subtracts the structured mean rounding error from the activation and weight gradients while leaving the optimizer unchanged. In LLM pre-training experiments, uncorrected threshold sharing degrades convergence, whereas S3R-EC eliminates this degradation and matches the validation loss of independent SR. Furthermore, S3R-EC accelerates full INT8 training steps of dense LLMs on TPU v5p by 1.24x to 1.32x over BF16 and by 1.11x over independent SR.
authors: Zeyu Wang, Yiheng Duan, Tao Chen, Donghyun Koo, Sihan Liu, Wenbo Zhang, Chuan He, Liang Liu
bullets: Independent stochastic rounding is costly because generating one random threshold per gradient element bottlenecks accelerator vector units.
Naively sharing thresholds reduces randomness overhead but introduces a common rounding offset that harms convergence through activation gradients.
S3R quantizes each upstream gradient once for both activation and weight computations, sharing one threshold per token across hidden dimensions.
S3R-EC removes the resulting structured mean rounding error without changing the optimizer.
In LLM pre-training on TPU v5p, S3R-EC matches independent-SR validation loss and achieves 1.24–1.32× speedup over BF16 and 1.11× over independent SR.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces structured subspace stochastic rounding to accelerate low-precision training, fitting the efficient-AI scope.
papers.title: Efficient Quantization Training with Stochastic Rounding via Structured Subspace Randomness
papers.tldr: S3R-EC makes stochastic rounding practical for fast full-INT8 LLM training by sharing token-level randomness while correcting its structured rounding bias.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are being applied to Web data streams such as network intrusion detection, where they adapt by updating the labelled rows of their context without retraining. When a past concept returns after leaving the context, a TFM faces a recall-or-relearn decision between restoring stored rows of the concept and relearning it from new labels. We propose MICE (Mixture of In-Context Experts), a training-free learner that cuts the stream into segments at detected changes. It merges a closed segment into a stored context when the TFM's estimated additional error on the segment is within a tolerance, under a capacity limit on stored contexts. A fast level weights the stored contexts and first-in-first-out (FIFO) windows by the log-loss of their predictions on the last labelled batch. We show that, with pure stored contexts and a margin condition, this fast level gains over relearning, in expected accuracy, the normalised positive area between the stored context's accuracy and the TFM's learning curve, up to a first-batch term. A slow level mixes the fast level's prediction with that of the FIFO window of the last labelled rows and bounds the discounted half-Brier regret of MICE against this window at every time. Learning curves measured beforehand predict the ordering of the observed recall gains. MICE outperforms reset, which empties the context at detected drifts, on grid streams with random boundary phases. Merging keeps fewer experts than pools that store every segment, and with fixed segmentation a time-matched snapshot pool matches MICE on the shifted grid. On real streams, MICE has the highest mean accuracy of all policies we compare.
authors: Zhangkai Wu, Xu Zhang, Zhihong Cui, Yiqi Wang, Yi Zhang
bullets: Addresses TFMs’ recall-versus-relearning decision when previously seen concepts return after leaving context.
Segments streams at detected changes and selectively merges segments into a capacity-limited pool of stored contexts.
Uses a fast log-loss weighting level over stored contexts and FIFO windows, plus a slower mixture with the latest labelled rows.
Theory links recall gains to stored-context accuracy and learning curves, and bounds discounted half-Brier regret against a recent-data baseline.
Outperforms context-reset policies on grid streams and achieves the highest mean accuracy among compared policies on real streams; fixed-segmentation snapshots can match it on shifted grids.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free in-context mixture for recurring concept drift, directly relevant to continual/online adaptation of foundation models.
papers.title: Recall or Relearn? A Mixture of In-Context Experts for Recurring Concept Drift
papers.tldr: MICE is a training-free strategy for recurring concept drift that adaptively recalls stored contexts or relearns from recent data, improving recall and accuracy across synthetic and real streams.

papers.abstract: To generate landmark-based route instructions, models must understand both map geometry and human landmark preferences. Although large language models (LLMs) show great abilities in language tasks, the best way to structure map data for these models is not yet established. This paper proposes a structured text representation for landmark selection tasks in route navigation, utilizing SVG format to encode spatial features. The structured text maintains a geometric connection with rendered map images, allowing language models to directly access spatial and semantic data. Using a new dataset created from human-written route descriptions and OpenStreetMap data, we evaluate models on two tasks: landmark selection at turns and around destinations. Experiments with five LLMs show that the proposed structured text input performs as well as or better than image-based PNG inputs. In addition, task-specific fine-tuning enables smaller local LLMs to effectively leverage map layouts to achieve high selection accuracy. These results demonstrate that structured text is an efficient and lightweight interface for spatial reasoning in human-oriented navigation.
authors: Mifu Matsumoto, Yuki Nakanishi, Tomoya Hashiguchi, Hiroaki Ohshima
bullets: Addresses the challenge of representing map geometry and semantic information for landmark-based route instruction generation.
Encodes spatial features in structured SVG text while preserving alignment with rendered map images.
Evaluates landmark selection at turns and near destinations using a dataset combining human-written routes with OpenStreetMap data.
Across five LLMs, structured text performs as well as or better than PNG map inputs.
Task-specific fine-tuning allows smaller local LLMs to use map layouts effectively.
papers.selection_reason: Encodes map geometry as structured text for LLM-based landmark selection, directly relevant to spatial reasoning and navigation instruction generation.
papers.title: Structured Maps for Landmark-Based Route Instructions with LLMs
papers.tldr: An SVG-based structured text representation helps LLMs select human-preferred landmarks for navigation as effectively as, or better than, map images.

papers.abstract: Final-answer accuracy reports whether a vision-language model was right, but not whether its answer was grounded in the image, whether its stated reasoning reflects that evidence, or what the answer cost to produce. Those are the properties that decide whether a system can be deployed. We present PRISM-BENCH, a benchmark of 1,000 expert-curated questions spanning five under-represented reasoning categories, in which every item carries an idealized reasoning trace written by one human annotator and validated by another. The traces support two diagnostics that accuracy cannot provide. A perception probe, in which the model answers from a description it wrote itself, attributes roughly 85% of frontier-model failures to misperception and places the bottleneck at grounding. Trace alignment predicts answer correctness for all 25 systems tested (macro AUROC 0.66) and survives length control, so it measures reasoning content and not verbosity. We further introduce CORE, an efficiency-aware metric that reorders 24.2% of model pairs relative to accuracy while remaining uncorrelated with response length. Across 25 open and closed systems, including GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.6, the best accuracy is 66.0%. On the four categories with a human baseline the best system trails humans by 18.4 points, and recent frontier gains fall on recognition and not on spatial grounding.
authors: Vansh Bhatia, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Parsa Ashrafi Fashi, Igor Gilitschenski, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Introduces 1,000 expert-curated questions across five under-represented reasoning categories, each with a validated ideal reasoning trace.
A self-description perception probe attributes roughly 85% of frontier-model failures to misperception, identifying grounding as the main bottleneck.
Trace alignment predicts correctness across all 25 evaluated systems, beyond effects of response length.
CORE, an efficiency-aware metric, reorders 24.2% of model pairs relative to accuracy while remaining uncorrelated with response length.
The best system reaches 66.0% accuracy, trails humans by 18.4 points where comparable, and recent gains emphasize recognition over spatial grounding.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for diagnosing grounded and faithful multimodal reasoning, providing metrics beyond final answer accuracy for VLMs.
papers.title: PRISM-BENCH: Diagnosing Grounded and Faithful Multimodal Reasoning Beyond Final-Answer Accuracy
papers.tldr: PRISM-BENCH shows that multimodal reasoning quality depends on grounding, faithful reasoning, and efficiency—not final-answer accuracy alone.

papers.abstract: Handwritten civil-status registers across Sub-Saharan Africa are being photographed, but rarely transcribed, which leaves their content unsearchable. Local administrations that hold these records typically lack GPUs, reliable connectivity, and the budget for external digitization services. We study whether a frugal pipeline, with consumer-grade capture and CPU-only inference, can make such registers machine-readable. We introduce a corpus of 1,568 smartphone images of handwritten birth, marriage, and death records from a municipal registry in Chad, with line-level transcriptions for 185 records. Our pipeline combines a fully classical preprocessing stage, running at about 2.6 images per second on a laptop CPU, with a Kraken recognizer fine-tuned from a pretrained model in about four hours on a free-tier GPU. On manually corrected line segmentation and a single-registry test set whose writers also appear in training, fine-tuning reduces the character error rate from 14.53% to 0.50% and the word error rate from 56.93% to 3.37%. On a six-core laptop CPU, the recognizer weighs 61 MiB, peaks below 2.6 GiB of RAM, and processes an image in under 6 s on average, excluding line segmentation. Finally, a downstream information-extraction task shows that residual recognition errors cost about 9 F1 points on role resolution, compared with a 36.7-point gap between the fine-tuned and pretrained recognizers. These results are evidence of feasibility within one registry, not of performance on unseen writers or sites; we discuss these limitations in detail.
authors: Ousmane Hamadou, Jean Louis Kedieng Ebongue Fendji
bullets: Targets digitization barriers in Sub-Saharan administrations lacking GPUs, reliable connectivity, and external-service budgets.
Introduces 1,568 smartphone images from 185 handwritten birth, marriage, and death records in a Chadian municipal registry, with line transcriptions.
Combines classical preprocessing with a Kraken recognizer fine-tuned on a pretrained model; inference runs on a laptop CPU without a GPU.
On manually corrected segmentation and a same-writer test setting, fine-tuning reduces character error rate from 14.53% to 0.50% and word error rate from 56.93% to 3.37%.
Residual recognition errors reduce downstream role-resolution F1 by about 9 points; results demonstrate feasibility only within the studied registry.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a frugal pipeline for handwritten text recognition that optimizes for CPU-only inference and memory usage, relevant to memory efficiency.
papers.title: Frugal Handwritten Text Recognition for Sub-Saharan Civil-Status Registers: A Smartphone-to-Records Pipeline with CPU-Only Inference
papers.tldr: A frugal smartphone-to-CPU pipeline can make handwritten civil-status records searchable within a single registry, but its strong accuracy has not been validated on unseen writers or sites.

papers.abstract: Humans are dexterous, but traditional data collection paradigms such as teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and wearable exoskeletons force humans to act through the robot embodiment, bottlenecking their dexterity. Retargeting can avoid this. However, existing methods purely translate kinematics and ignore the real-world contact dynamics essential for task success. We present CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation, a simulator and object-free framework that retargets human demonstrations to robot actions by explicitly preserving contact force targets. CARD unifies human data sources including video, motion capture, and tactile gloves via a shared hand--contact representation and generates explicit contact force targets in addition to kinematics. To maintain these contact targets during hardware open-loop replay, CARD also introduces a tactile tracking controller. For video which does not contain an explicit tactile source, we present Vid-HACO, our video-to-contact model that sets a new state of the art. Across our video, glove, motion-capture data and the GRAB dataset, CARD maintains contact on $43$--$78\%$ of contact frames, while kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on $<10\%$ and $22.5\%$ of the frames respectively. Further, integrating our formulation into physics-based retargeting improves strict task success from 12\% to 32\% on GRAB dataset. Finally, we show that our tactile tracker is critical to reproduce demonstrated forces during hardware replay. These results establish that contact preservation via CARD is a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.
authors: Cunxi Dai, Botao He, Francois R Hogan, Wei Pan, Rao Fu, Wen-Han Hsieh, Ruoshi Liu, Jitendra Malik, Guanya Shi, Akash Sharma
bullets: Addresses the failure of kinematics-only retargeting to preserve the contact dynamics needed for successful manipulation.
Uses a shared hand–contact representation for video, motion capture, and tactile-glove data, generating both robot actions and contact-force targets.
Introduces Vid-HACO for inferring contacts from video and a tactile tracking controller for hardware open-loop replay.
Maintains contact on 43–78% of contact frames, compared with under 10% for kinematic and 22.5% for object-aware retargeting.
Improves strict task success on GRAB from 12% to 32% when integrated with physics-based retargeting; hardware results show tactile tracking is essential for reproducing forces.
papers.selection_reason: Contact-anchored retargeting of human demonstrations to dexterous manipulation, including video-to-contact model; strongly relevant to robot manipulation and learning from human video.
papers.title: CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: CARD retargets human dexterous manipulation to robots by preserving contact forces—not just hand kinematics—across multiple demonstration modalities.

papers.abstract: We present CPG-ENN, a trainable quadruped locomotion framework that combines explicit neural coordination with learned motion realization. A symmetry-based eight-neuron central pattern generator (CPG) supplies gait rhythms, while a pretrained, leg-shared execution neural network (ENN) maps rhythmic signals and trajectory parameters to joint-angle references without online inverse kinematics. A single feedback policy modulates six physically interpretable trajectory variables. The controller tracks planar velocity and yaw-rate commands across walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk without gait-specific learned controllers or transitionspecific rewards. Simulation yields 99.39% transition success across all 20 directed gait pairs and all source-target speed combinations from {0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0} m/s. Ablations show high cross-gait transition feasibility without transition exposure; exposure mainly refines gait acquisition and velocity transients. Comparisons with AllGaits and Walk These Ways demonstrate accurate gait-speed regulation, and Unitree Go2 experiments validate five gaits and their transitions.
authors: Xiyan Liu, Yide Liu, Guoyong Mao, Shaoxing Qu
bullets: Targets robust velocity and yaw-rate control across walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk.
Uses an eight-neuron CPG for gait rhythms and a pretrained leg-shared ENN to generate joint-angle references.
A feedback policy adjusts six physically interpretable trajectory variables.
Simulation achieved 99.39% transition success across 20 directed gait pairs and tested speed combinations.
Experiments on a Unitree Go2 validated all five gaits and their transitions; transition exposure mainly improved gait acquisition and velocity transients.
papers.selection_reason: Trainable CPG framework for quadruped locomotion with learned execution network; directly relevant to legged robot control.
papers.title: A Trainable CPG Framework for Quadruped Locomotion
papers.tldr: CPG-ENN combines a symmetry-based CPG, shared neural motion execution, and feedback control to produce and transition among five quadruped gaits without gait-specific transition training or online inverse kinematics.

papers.abstract: Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models.
authors: Bozhao Wang, Yinglei Zhu, Zhengqing Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Weiming Kang, Yiheng He, XinJun Liu, Senhao Hou, Huichan Zhao, Xiaoqiang Tang
bullets: Addresses policy reuse challenges caused by differences in musculoskeletal morphology.
Combines individualized model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning, and virtual model augmentation.
Achieves 99.24% completion across 31 held-out models and reduces tracking error by 22.60% versus an unconditioned MLP.
Generalizes to single-image-based models and models with unilateral lower-limb shortening.
Simulations agree with measured ground-reaction forces and show channel-dependent agreement with electromyography.
papers.selection_reason: Morphology-conditioned generalist policy for muscle-driven control; transferable learning-based control across embodied models.
papers.title: A generalist policy for muscle-driven control across individual musculoskeletal models
papers.tldr: MyoAcross enables one muscle-driven control policy to track reference movements across diverse individual musculoskeletal models without per-model fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Attention Matching (AM) compacts a KV cache by keeping some keys per head, refitting their values and adding a bias to each kept key's logit. FlashAttention and vLLM's paged caches have no input for it. We fold the bias into the keys along one closed-form direction per head, fitted on context queries, giving a plain cache with AM's size and head dimension and the model's own query path; the output error is bounded by how far each query's projection on that direction is from 1. With equal per-head budgets, unmodified vLLM serves folded caches through a KV connector, matching Hugging Face's answers on all 51 Qwen3-4B questions and its greedy output on 180 of 200 Qwen3-14B LongBench samples. With equal budgets on QuALITY (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 8B, Llama-3.1-8B) and LongHealth (three Qwen3 models), the fold is within noise of AM's accuracy in 13 of 14 settings, with lower KL to the full cache than dropping the bias in all 12 where both ran. Under the published per-head budgets, on Qwen3-4B, its Instruct-2507 variant and Llama-3.1-8B, it is within noise of AM in 9 of 10, no longer beats dropping the bias in KL, and the two each win once in accuracy.
bullets: AM compresses KV caches by retaining selected keys, refitting values, and adding per-key logit biases—but standard kernels cannot consume those biases.
The proposed closed-form, per-head key adjustment absorbs each bias along one fitted direction, preserving the model’s normal query path and cache dimensions.
Unmodified vLLM serves the folded caches through a KV connector; outputs closely match Hugging Face and retain most greedy generations in the reported tests.
Across equal-budget evaluations, folding matches AM within noise in 13 of 14 settings and generally produces lower KL divergence than omitting the bias.
Under published per-head budgets, folding remains comparable to AM in 9 of 10 settings, though its KL advantage disappears.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses KV cache compaction and memory-efficient inference by folding attention biases into keys.
papers.title: Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels
papers.tldr: Folding Attention Matching’s key biases into the keys enables compact KV caches to run on standard FlashAttention/vLLM kernels with nearly unchanged accuracy.

papers.abstract: Agentic life-science benchmarks give an agent evidence about a named entity and score an answer against a recorded outcome. That score tests reasoning over evidence only if the evidence, rather than the name, determines the answer. We examine this distinction by varying identity and evidence independently on a clinical-outcome benchmark and published tasks from Biomni and LAB-Bench. Blinding identity matters little when a prompt contains a decisive sequence or passage. It matters a great deal when the prompt is mostly a name and candidate list (0.742 named versus 0.082 blinded; chance 0.093). Across 96 LAB-Bench LitQA2 questions, the gap increases under one fixed passage-redaction scheme (+0.000 to +0.135; per-instance slope +0.147, p= 0.004). On the clinical benchmark, a no-evidence recall probe matches prediction accuracy and recovers a database-specific programme count. So, we argue that benchmarks intended to measure evidence-dependent reasoning should report identity-blinded results, retrieval telemetry, and positive controls.
bullets: The study independently varies entity identity and provided evidence on a clinical-outcome benchmark and Biomni/LAB-Bench tasks.
Identity blinding has little effect when prompts contain decisive sequences or passages, but greatly reduces performance for name-and-candidate-list prompts (0.742 to 0.082; chance 0.093).
Across 96 LAB-Bench LitQA2 questions, performance gaps increased under passage redaction, with a reported per-instance slope of +0.147 (p=0.004).
A no-evidence recall probe on the clinical benchmark matched prediction accuracy and recovered a database-specific programme count.
The authors recommend identity-blinded evaluation, retrieval telemetry, and positive controls for benchmarks measuring evidence-dependent reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Audits LLM benchmarks to distinguish between identity-based and evidence-based reasoning, providing insights into LLM evaluation and reasoning mechanisms.
papers.title: Identity or Evidence? Auditing Evidence Dependence in Agentic Life-Science Benchmarks
papers.tldr: Many agentic life-science benchmarks may reward recognizing entity names rather than reasoning from evidence, especially when evidence is sparse.

papers.abstract: Multimodal forgery detection is commonly studied under a static assumption: training attacks are expected to approximate those encountered after deployment. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile as generators, editing systems, and multimodal large language models continually introduce new forgery mechanisms and forensic evidence. We formulate this problem as attack-incremental continual multimodal forgery detection, where the binary real/fake interface remains fixed while emerging attacks must be learned without forgetting previous ones. We introduce Fable-Bench, which organizes attack evolution through complementary joint-modality, text-side, and image-side protocols. We further propose ARISE (Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement), motivated by the open-ended forged class and the comparatively reusable geometry of authentic content. ARISE fits a real-only Gaussian mixture model to projected authentic replay representations as a compact historical reference. Meanwhile, the proposed Gaussian-Responsibility-Aware Stability Preservation (GRASP) derives a sample-adaptive anisotropic metric that strongly constrains historically stable representation directions while retaining plasticity elsewhere. Our Vulnerability-Aware Replay (VAR) further estimates stage-wise vulnerability from authentic-density degradation, forged-to-authentic boundary confusion, and authentic-mode occupancy drift, then assigns bounded replay emphasis to fragile stages. All adaptive signals are obtained from training-time replay statistics, while inference uses only the original multimodal backbone and binary classification head. Experiments across three attack-evolution protocols and multiple detector architectures demonstrate improved historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Yaxiong Wang, Yujiao Wu, Lianwei Wu, Qi Zhang, Li Zhu, Chaofeng Dong, Le Wu, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Addresses attack-incremental detection, where new forgery mechanisms appear without changing the real/fake interface and prior knowledge must be retained.
Introduces Fable-Bench with joint-modality, text-side, and image-side attack-evolution protocols.
Models authentic replay representations with a real-only Gaussian mixture and uses GRASP for sample-adaptive stability–plasticity control.
Uses VAR to prioritize replay for stages vulnerable to authentic-density degradation, boundary confusion, or mode drift.
Across three protocols and multiple detector architectures, ARISE improves historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses continual learning for multimodal forgery detection, introducing stability preservation mechanisms to handle evolving attack patterns.
papers.title: ARISE: Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement for Continual Multimodal Forgery Detection
papers.tldr: ARISE improves continual multimodal forgery detection by preserving authentic-content representations while adapting to newly emerging attacks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.
authors: Liang Li, Guoyao Zhang, Xingyu Chen, Sikai Wu, Qianyang Wu, Yuhang Lin, Renjing Xu, Mingliang Zhou, Diyun Xiang
bullets: Targets missing terrain adaptation in flat-ground-trained behavior foundation models, especially foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing.
Adds a terrain-conditioned residual adapter that modifies only lower-body execution targets while preserving the frozen tracker and reference interface.
Trains with task and foot-geometry rewards, suppresses unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distills privileged terrain information to onboard depth.
Evaluated on four frozen trackers across stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation.
Demonstrated real-world terrain traversal on a Unitree G1 using the adapted SONIC tracker, onboard depth, and unmodified references.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware residual adaptation for frozen humanoid behavior trackers; learned terrain-conditioned control relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: GRAFT: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Foundation Trackers
papers.tldr: GRAFT adapts frozen humanoid behavior trackers to uneven terrain by learning lightweight, geometry-aware lower-body corrections from depth without retraining the underlying tracker.

papers.abstract: Web fashion images support applications such as visual product search and consumer-to-shop matching, yet their visual heterogeneity makes reliable garment segmentation challenging. Despite advances in promptable segmentation, autonomously identifying and correcting garment-specific errors without human-provided spatial prompts remains difficult. We propose GarmentSegAgent, an autonomous framework that integrates semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation through iterative textual self-refinement. At its core, we introduce CAST (Constrained Attribution-guided Selective TextGrad), which connects visual error attribution with targeted textual optimization. CAST identifies instruction components responsible for segmentation errors, selectively updates them through textual gradients, and validates the resulting instructions against garment-specific constraints. This enables image-specific error correction at inference time while keeping the underlying foundation models frozen. Experiments on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia demonstrate consistent improvements in region overlap and boundary accuracy, alongside more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad. By enabling visual feedback to guide controlled instruction updates, GarmentSegAgent offers a promising direction for autonomous garment understanding, with potential applications in scalable fashion content analysis, visual retrieval, and consumer-to-shop matching on the Web.
authors: Jia Chen, Chao Huang, Xinrong Hu, Mingdi Huang, Ruyang Zhao, Jun Bai
bullets: Addresses unreliable garment segmentation caused by heterogeneous web fashion imagery and the need for spatial prompts.
Combines semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation in an iterative self-refinement framework.
Introduces CAST, which attributes errors to instruction components, selectively optimizes them, and checks garment-specific constraints.
Evaluations on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia show consistent gains in region overlap and boundary accuracy, with more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad.
Foundation models remain frozen; refinement occurs at inference time through image-specific instruction updates.
papers.selection_reason: Utilizes textual self-refinement to autonomously correct segmentation errors at inference time, fitting the test-time learning paradigm.
papers.title: GarmentSegAgent: Autonomous Garment Segmentation for Web Fashion Images via Textual Self-Refinement
papers.tldr: GarmentSegAgent autonomously improves garment segmentation in diverse web fashion images by refining textual instructions from visual error feedback, without human prompts or model fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Video models answer from sampled frames and may miss the decisive moment. A common remedy is to commit to an answer, re-examine the video, and confirm or revise it, a loop now mainly learned with reinforcement learning (RL). We find that RL erodes the initial answer, a phenomenon we term confidence erosion, where confidence means the label-verified reliability of the initial answer instead of self-reported certainty: because errors can be repaired later, a correct initial answer earns less reward, and the initial answer stalls even as the final answer's gain over it rises. We propose the principle confident first, reflective second: the initial answer must stay reliable on its own, above a floor set by a reference policy, and reflection may only add to it. Our method, CoFire, implements this principle with one mechanism for each erosion channel: reward incentives, parameter drift, and gradient interference. CoFire reaches 67.0% mean accuracy on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, 1.7 points above the strongest compared 7B method, and improves initial-answer and final accuracy over outcome-reward RL by 4.1 and 3.7 points on average: a stronger initial answer carries through to a stronger final one.
authors: Zihao Lin, Jingyuan Liu, Yucheng Zhang, Yuguang Yao, Lifu Huang
bullets: RL-based reflection can cause confidence erosion: correct initial answers are undervalued because later correction is rewarded.
CoFire enforces a reference-policy reliability floor for the initial answer and allows reflection to add, not replace, its value.
It addresses reward incentives, parameter drift, and gradient interference as sources of erosion.
CoFire achieves 67.0% mean accuracy across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, 1.7 points above the strongest compared 7B method.
Compared with outcome-reward RL, it improves initial and final accuracy by 4.1 and 3.7 points on average.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses video understanding by using reinforcement learning to refine answers through reflection, specifically tackling confidence erosion in video models.
papers.title: Confident First, Reflective Second: Reinforcement Learning of Confidence-Preserving Reflection for Video Understanding
papers.tldr: CoFire trains video models to answer reliably before reflection, preserving initial-answer quality while still improving final answers through re-examination.

papers.abstract: We propose Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni (NLD-Uni), a unified discrete diffusion large language model (DLLM) for visual understanding and generation tasks. Compared with prior unified diffusion models, NLD-Uni introduces two major innovations. First, we propose a unified cross-paradigm on-policy distillation (OPD) framework that successfully transfers the visual understanding ability of autoregressive VLMs and visual generation ability of continuous flow models, to a unified DLLM. Second, NLD-Uni incorporates a novel progressive self-refining diffusion process that gradually corrupts each token across multiple steps during training, as opposed to adopting the conventional masked diffusion formulation that directly corrupts a clean image token to an uninformative mask token. At inference, this design allows NLD-Uni to make intermediate commit to a token, enabling progressive self-refinement for better visual quality. Through extensive experiments, we show that NLD-Uni achieves state-of-the-art performance among unified DLLMs on diverse tasks including visual question-answering, multi-modal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.
authors: Shufan Li, Hanrong Ye, Greg Heinrich, Yonggan Fu, Haotian Zhang, Sifei Liu, Aditya Grover, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Transfers capabilities from autoregressive vision-language models and continuous flow models into one unified diffusion model.
Uses cross-paradigm on-policy distillation to train visual understanding and generation abilities.
Introduces progressive self-refining diffusion, gradually corrupting tokens instead of replacing them directly with masks.
Enables intermediate token commitments during inference for progressive visual refinement.
Reports state-of-the-art unified-DLLM performance across VQA, multimodal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified discrete diffusion LLM that bridges visual understanding and generation through cross-paradigm distillation and self-refining processes.
papers.title: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni: Elastic Self-Refining Unified Diffusion LLM with Cross-Paradigm On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: NLD-Uni is a unified discrete diffusion language model that combines visual understanding and generation through cross-paradigm distillation and progressive self-refinement.

papers.abstract: We study 3D visual grounding in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where a referring expression should identify a target object as both a rendered 2D mask and a set of explicit 3D Gaussians. Prior methods typically extract 3D targets by applying heuristic thresholding or top-ratio filtering to dense primitive-level relevance scores. However, these scores often vary substantially across scenes and prompts, making such heuristics sensitive and leading to unstable targeting. ClusterSplat addresses this by reframing 3D target selection as cluster-level selection over scene-adaptive candidates. The method first learns instance-aware Gaussian features, forms feature-aware seed voxels, and merges neighboring seed voxels when a description-length criterion decreases, producing a scene-specific set of cluster candidates. Given a referring expression, a query-conditioned cluster scorer ranks the cluster candidates with a lightweight MLP, and the selected cluster directly defines the explicit 3D target while its cluster score is rendered for the 2D mask. On ScanRefer, ClusterSplat achieves the best rendered 2D segmentation and explicit 3D target metrics among the compared 3DGS baselines. It also obtains the best average Ref-LERF scores, supporting the same trend under fine-grained referring descriptions. On ScanNet v2 class name queries, ClusterSplat achieves the strongest rendered 2D results and the highest 3D matching accuracy, while maintaining competitive 3D IoU. Our project page is available at https://jaesung8.github.io/clustersplat/ .
authors: Jaesung Lee, Hyeontaek Hwang, Gabriel Manalu, Daeyoung Kim
bullets: Targets referring expressions as both rendered 2D masks and explicit sets of 3D Gaussians.
Learns instance-aware features, builds feature-aware seed voxels, and merges them using a description-length criterion.
Uses a query-conditioned lightweight MLP to rank cluster candidates and select the 3D target.
Reports the best results among compared 3DGS baselines on multiple 2D and 3D grounding metrics across ScanRefer and ScanNet v2.
Scope: performance is evaluated on referring descriptions and class-name queries in indoor 3D scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces 3D visual grounding in 3D Gaussian Splatting, a 3D foundation representation method, addressing target selection in 3D scenes.
papers.title: ClusterSplat: Semantic Cluster Selection for 3D Visual Grounding in Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: ClusterSplat improves 3D visual grounding in Gaussian Splatting by selecting scene-adaptive semantic clusters instead of relying on unstable primitive-level thresholds.

papers.abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.
authors: Alexa R. Tartaglini, Zhengxuan Wu, Thadd\"aus Wiedemer, Martin Wattenberg, Been Kim, Yuxuan Li
bullets: Simple symbols, such as a red heart, can implicitly steer VLM behavior toward recursive solutions on coding tasks.
Models’ stated interpretations and reasoning about symbols may differ substantially from the behavior those symbols induce.
Visual communication between models shows a generation–interpretation gap: intuitive shape-based cues often fail to steer other models.
In communication games, VLMs can creatively convey abstract concepts and stories, though some messages are unintuitive to humans.
The work highlights both the promise and challenges of human–VLM visual communication.
papers.selection_reason: Explores visual meaning and communication in vision-language models, directly relevant to multimodal large language models.
papers.title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs
papers.tldr: VLMs can use visuals to influence behavior and communicate abstract meaning, but their visual interpretations and conventions often diverge from both humans and other models.

papers.abstract: Traditional multiple sclerosis (MS) image analysis has primarily focused on retrospectively detecting and segmenting lesions. This study investigates whether baseline FLAIR MRI can identify regions at risk for future lesion formation beyond population-level spatial patterns. We introduce FORESEE-MS, an evaluation protocol that uses a fold-specific population-prior atlas as a baseline and assesses predictions using pooled voxel-level discrimination (AUROC and AUPRC) and within-patient lesion localization (Recall@Top-K%), with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. We evaluated five deep learning models (3D U-Net, Attn+ResBlock+VAE, ViT, and two SwinUNETR variants) using 5-fold cross-validation on 39 subjects from the MSSEG-2 dataset. The atlas achieved the highest pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC, with no deep learning model reliably outperforming it on either metric. However, the 3D U-Net and Attn+ResBlock+VAE achieved higher mean voxel-level within-patient Recall@Top-K% than the atlas at all evaluated thresholds, although most paired confidence intervals for the differences included zero. These findings suggest that baseline FLAIR may contain patient-specific predictive information, but in this small cohort, it remains uncertain whether this information improves lesion forecasting beyond a population-prior atlas.
authors: Maryam Akhavan Aghdam, Sudip Mittal, Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Shahram Rahimi
bullets: Tests prospective lesion forecasting rather than retrospective lesion detection or segmentation.
Compares five deep learning models with a fold-specific population-prior atlas using voxel-level discrimination and within-patient localization metrics.
Evaluates models with 5-fold cross-validation on 39 subjects from the MSSEG-2 dataset.
The atlas performed best on pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC, while 3D U-Net and Attn+ResBlock+VAE had higher mean within-patient Recall@Top-K%.
Most paired confidence intervals included zero, so improvement over the atlas remains uncertain in this small cohort.
papers.selection_reason: Predicts future 3D states (lesions) from baseline MRI using deep learning, aligning with the concept of environment dynamics forecasting in world models.
papers.title: FORESEE-MS: Toward Prospective Spatial Forecasting of Future Multiple Sclerosis Lesions from Baseline FLAIR MRI
papers.tldr: FORESEE-MS evaluates whether baseline FLAIR MRI can predict future MS lesion locations beyond a population-prior atlas, finding suggestive but inconclusive patient-specific predictive information.

papers.abstract: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.
bullets: Targets low-cost SO-101 arms, addressing the lack of accessible benchmarks for spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks.
Provides four tasks across five evaluation families, 138 objects, seen/unseen splits, 916 episodes, and simulated demonstrations in an Isaac Lab digital twin.
Policy rankings in simulation exactly matched physical-robot rankings for five policies tested, though simulation overestimated success.
Best learned policies achieved about 61%, while an LLM code-writing agent paired with a learned grasping policy reached 83.2%.
Spatial placement, unseen object classes, and rotate-to-fit planning remain open challenges.
papers.selection_reason: Simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation on low-cost arms, evaluating VLAs and LLM agents; directly embodied manipulation and VLA.
papers.title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation
papers.tldr: SO-101 Bench is a simulated, language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark whose digital twin reliably ranks policies but exposes substantial challenges in generalization, planning, and spatial placement.

papers.abstract: Compact electroencephalography (EEG) decoders enable embedded brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but compression can alter adversarial robustness without proportional hardware savings. We present ORBITAL, a robustness-constrained framework combining hardware-realizable structured compression, recovery-aware operating-point selection, multi-attack evaluation, and native edge validation. Across nine subjects and three seeds on BCI Competition IV-2a, S25-TRADES achieves the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models (23.06% vs 21.27% for standard Full), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. Matched controls identify TRADES as the main source of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy by 6.74 percentage points over clean recovery (p=0.0039), while per-example analysis reveals boundary redistribution rather than uniform margin expansion. On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduces board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%. Despite 99.3% prediction agreement, native INT8 Q/DQ incurs about twice the FP16 latency and energy, demonstrating the need for joint robustness and hardware-aware optimization.
bullets: Structured compression can change adversarial robustness without matching hardware gains.
S25-TRADES achieved the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models, while reducing parameters and MACs versus Full.
TRADES was the main driver of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy over clean recovery in matched controls.
On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduced energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%.
Native INT8 Q/DQ showed roughly twice the FP16 latency and energy despite 99.3% prediction agreement, highlighting hardware-dependent trade-offs.
papers.selection_reason: Robustness-constrained low-precision compression for edge inference, reducing memory, energy, and latency; relevant to efficient AI via memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression
papers.tldr: ORBITAL jointly optimizes compressed EEG decoders for adversarial robustness and real edge-hardware efficiency, with FP16 compression offering the strongest practical trade-off.

papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories couple a learned design surrogate to an instrument, and on every new target domain it must answer four questions: when it can be trusted, how many target measurements it needs, which to make first, and when to stop adapting, switch models or escalate. We state a framework making each measurable (a competence ratio, a budget $k^*(\varepsilon)$, a time-to-target and a priced decision) and instantiate it without wet experiments on six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables as offline laboratories: 107 leave-one-group tiers whose rows are hidden labels. A sealed, pre-registered programme (two sealed negative validations and a pre-registered test on three more tables) and seven frozen closed-loop protocols, each run twice, yield 23 findings. Shift cost is stratified by shift type; no label-free statistic certifies individual candidates; random-split model-family rankings predicted neither the sealed nor the loop rankings. Warm-start residual boosting returns a surrogate to $1.25\times$ its development reference within 20 target rows in 94% of chemistry tiers (27% under a strict noise-floor reading), 90% of laboratory and 40% of device tiers, and a budget planned from the shift type on other tables is not measurably worse on a new one. In the loop, one gain survives drift and shuffled-label controls on all tiers, carried by the sparsely sampled ones: proposing at once and warm-starting on every measurement reaches a 10% target in 2.80 measurements against 3.31 for the reference, and in 5.72 against 11.35 for random proposals on 301 hard units at a 3% tolerance. No label-free acquisition rule survives the shuffled-label control, no interval-aware proposal or other model family does better, and no threshold rule on the tested diagnostics beats always continuing once escalation is priced. No wet-lab validation is claimed.
bullets: Evaluated 107 leave-one-group tiers across six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables using sealed, preregistered offline protocols.
Formalized measurable trust, target-measurement budget, time-to-target, and cost-aware decisions for adapting, switching, or escalating a surrogate.
Warm-start residual boosting recovered near-reference performance within 20 target rows most often in chemistry tiers, less often in laboratory and device tiers.
Propose-then-update reached a 10% target in 2.80 versus 3.31 measurements for the reference, and 5.72 versus 11.35 for random proposals on hard units at 3% tolerance.
Shuffled-label controls invalidated label-free acquisition rules; no tested stopping threshold, interval-aware proposal, or alternative model family consistently improved decisions.
papers.selection_reason: Offline closed-loop framework for adapting learned surrogates on new target domains; relevant to test-time and continual adaptation.
papers.title: When Can a Learned Design Surrogate Be Trusted in a Self-Driving Microfluidics Laboratory? An Offline Closed-Loop Framework Built and Tested on Six Public Tables
papers.tldr: An offline study defines and tests when learned surrogates can be trusted and adapted in self-driving microfluidics, finding that warm-start closed-loop updating helps on sparse, shifted settings but no label-free stopping or acquisition rule is reliable.

papers.abstract: Modeling multi-scale dynamics in urban road networks is essential for intelligent transportation systems but is often hindered by the computational cost of long-range historical context and the challenge of fusing heterogeneous modalities. Existing spatio-temporal frameworks face a trade-off between sequence length and memory overhead, while frequently neglecting the transient effects of exogenous factors such as road incidents and weather. To address these limitations, we propose SpecLST, a frequency-enhanced long-short-term spatio-temporal multimodal framework. SpecLST leverages a fast Fourier transform-based frequency-domain representation module to efficiently encode multi-week historical dependencies, bypassing the memory bottlenecks of standard attention mechanisms over raw long sequences. Heterogeneous context is integrated through attention-based fusion, followed by a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone with graph augmentation for spatio-temporal representation learning. Additionally, a frequency-enhanced residual head isolates high-frequency transients, improving sensitivity to abrupt traffic anomalies. At the 60-minute horizon, SpecLST achieves mean relative error reductions of 14.10% in MAE, 10.35% in RMSE, and 15.78% in MAPE across eight neural forecasting baselines and four datasets, with the dataset- and metric-specific average reductions ranging from 5.63% to 22.21%.
authors: Kenan Kang, Matthew M. Y. Kuo, Weihua Li
bullets: Addresses the memory cost of long historical sequences and weak handling of heterogeneous, time-varying factors such as incidents and weather.
Uses FFT-based frequency representations to encode multi-week dependencies more efficiently than attention over raw long sequences.
Fuses heterogeneous context with attention, then applies a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone with graph augmentation.
Adds a frequency-enhanced residual head to capture high-frequency, abrupt traffic anomalies.
At a 60-minute horizon, reports average error reductions of 14.10% in MAE, 10.35% in RMSE, and 15.78% in MAPE across four datasets and eight baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Frequency-domain long-sequence encoding reduces memory overhead of attention; transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: SpecLST: Spectral-Enhanced Long-Short Term Spatio-Temporal Multimodal Modeling for Traffic Forecasting
papers.tldr: SpecLST combines frequency-domain long-term modeling, multimodal fusion, graph-enhanced sparse experts, and transient detection to improve multi-scale traffic forecasting.

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a key mechanism for efficiently specializing foundation models into many task- and user-specific variants. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank-distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.
bullets: LoRA fleet compression must allocate rank both across layers within adapters and across adapters under a shared budget.
The method builds per-adapter functional rank-distortion frontiers from isolated module truncation measurements and dynamic programming.
Complete candidates are re-evaluated end to end and combined with a spectral proposal before exact fleet-level minimax allocation.
Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget settings.
Isolated measurements rank candidates effectively, but calibration varies with proposal shape, making end-to-end verification important.
papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc LoRA adapter compression reduces memory/compute for serving many adapters, fitting the Efficient AI topic even without a specific subtopic.
papers.title: LoRA on a Budget: Function-Aware Post-Hoc Compression for Adapter Fleets
papers.tldr: FRA compresses fleets of LoRA adapters by allocating rank according to measured end-to-end functional degradation rather than spectral redundancy alone.

papers.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
authors: Matea Tashkovska, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Haozhe Qi, Alexander Mathis
bullets: Introduces 1,632 human-verified questions spanning body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning.
Evaluates 37 closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, alongside human evaluation.
Humans achieve 68.5% video-only accuracy, compared with 50.0% for the strongest evaluated MLLM, Qwen3.6-27B, in zero-shot evaluation.
Finds recurring errors in interpreting the wearer’s body, temporal events, repetition counts, and hand-side biases.
Provides aligned video–body-motion–language training data and a multimodal baseline to support future research.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and training data for egocentric body-motion and temporal reasoning in MLLMs; directly relevant to egocentric video learning and video understanding.
papers.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding
papers.tldr: SOMA benchmarks fine-grained body-motion understanding in egocentric video and reveals substantial gaps between current MLLMs and human performance.

papers.abstract: For efficiency, industrial large language model (LLM) labelers often pack many candidate labels into one prompt and generate a YES/NO answer for each, even when each decision depends only on the entity and one candidate. Generating these independent decisions as one answer list couples them, spends decoding on the list, and relies on the list being well-formed. In this paper, we present an end-to-end recipe that reformulates the labeler as semantic scoring, fine-tuning it on single-candidate prompts to return each decision as one answer-token score from a prefill-only pass. We also adapt Multiple-Item Scoring (MIS) to score hundreds of candidates in one sequence with attention masked between them. Deployed for profile qualification labeling at LinkedIn, semantic scoring changes at most 0.01% of decisions when candidates are reordered and matches the agreement with reference labels that packed generation reaches only with about 4.7x as many training pairs. The MIS-based stack raises throughput over the deployed stack by 1.24x offline and 1.9x in model serving under a one-second p99 latency target. For offline batch inference, we implement MIS-based scoring as a reusable, model-agnostic Ray Data API proposed for upstream adoption. Model serving uses MIS support contributed to SGLang.
